# Grinding Noise in Rear After Replacing Front Rotors/Pads

Replacing front brake components on a vehicle with rear drum brakes often feels like an isolated task, but mechanical systems are interconnected. If you are hearing a harsh grinding noise after freshening up the front end, specifically one that worsens at low speeds and persists briefly into acceleration, the issue is almost certainly not in the front. The sound originates from the rear passenger-side drums, likely triggered by a change in braking dynamics rather than damage to the rear assembly itself.

The correlation between changing front pads and hearing a new noise in the rear stems from how brake balance affects vehicle stability. When you replace rotors and pads on the front axle, you are altering the stopping force distribution. If the new front components offer significantly more friction or have a different wear characteristic than the old ones, the car may lock up the front wheels earlier than intended during moderate braking events.

This imbalance forces the driver to modulate braking pressure differently. In your specific case, the noise appears when slowing from 60mph to 30mph. At high speeds, kinetic energy is high, and even a slight over-application of brake pedal can lock the front wheels without causing immediate instability. However, as speed drops into that 30-40mph range, the vehicle becomes more sensitive to weight transfer. If the front brakes are now "grabby" or if the new rotor surface is uneven (common with direct replacement parts), the car might be pulling slightly or the driver might be instinctively easing off the pedal earlier than before to maintain control.

Rear drum brakes on a 2003 Corolla operate via an internal expanding mechanism actuated by wheel cylinders. When you brake, hydraulic pressure forces the pistons out, pushing shoes against the drum lining. If the front wheels are not applying sufficient pressure to hold the vehicle's weight distribution, the rear brakes might experience a different load profile. However, the primary suspect for a grinding noise that disappears when coasting is a mechanical engagement issue within the drum assembly, often exacerbated by the car sitting in a slightly different dynamic state.

A common culprit in this scenario is the parking brake (handbrake) cable or adjuster. On rear drum setups, the parking brake shoes are held back by springs but expanded by the cable when parked. If the front brakes have changed your braking feel, you might be relying more on the foot pedal for stopping power and less on the handbrake to hold the car on an incline. If the handbrake is not fully released, or if the cable has stretched further due to the increased reliance on mechanical holding force, the shoes could remain in partial contact with the drum lining.

This "drag" is often subtle at high speeds because the wheel spins faster, creating a thin film of heat and slight lubrication that reduces friction. As you slow down, the rotational velocity drops, increasing the effective friction coefficient until it becomes audible grinding. Once you release the foot brake to accelerate, the momentum overcomes the drag momentarily, or the shoe retracts slightly, silencing the noise until the next braking event increases the load again.

To diagnose this without disassembly immediately, check the parking brake adjuster. Locate the star wheel adjustment inside the rear drum (accessible by removing the drum). If the shoes are too close to the drum, they will drag. You can test this by jacking up the rear passenger wheel and spinning it by hand with the parking brake engaged. If it spins freely, the cable is likely fine, but if there is resistance or grinding, the shoe-to-drum clearance is insufficient.

Another possibility involves the wheel cylinders themselves. If fluid was contaminated or air introduced during the front job (less likely but possible if the master cylinder was bled differently), rear drag could manifest. However, given the description of the noise worsening at low speeds and persisting after braking, mechanical drag from the parking system is the most probable root cause linked to the changed front brake dynamics.

If you have verified the front installation is correct and the vehicle drives straight without pulling, focus entirely on the rear drum clearance and parking brake release mechanism. Adjusting the star wheel or replacing a seized cable is often all that is required to resolve the noise without needing new rotors or pads.
